t: Building H2O — Barrier Synchronization with Counting Semaphores
o: We must coordinate two thread types so they pass a barrier in groups of exactly one oxygen and two hydrogens, and all threads of one molecule release before the next molecule's threads do. In Example 1 (`HOH`), the hydrogen arriving first must block until an oxygen and another hydrogen arrive; then all three call their release functions. In Example 2 (`OOHHHH`), the second oxygen must wait until the first molecule (one O + two H) has fully bonded, even though it arrived early. The constraints guarantee exact counts (2n H, n O), so we never need to handle starvation from missing atoms — only correct grouping and ordering. This is a classic concurrency problem solved with semaphores/mutexes acting as counters.
k: A semaphore counting available hydrogens (initialized to 2) plus a mutex/semaphore for oxygen enforces the 2:1 ratio per molecule.
The last thread to join a molecule resets the counters, guaranteeing each group of three completes before the next begins.
Order of release calls within a molecule is free; only the barrier between molecules matters.

a.i: Use a hydrogen semaphore initialized to 2: each hydrogen acquires one permit, so at most two hydrogens can be 'in' a molecule before permits run out. Oxygen uses a binary semaphore (or mutex) so only one oxygen joins per molecule. Track how many threads have joined the current molecule; the third thread (which knows the molecule is complete) releases everything: it signals the hydrogen semaphore twice and the oxygen semaphore once, refilling permits for the next molecule.
s: Initialize hSem = Semaphore(2), oSem = Semaphore(1), and a counter of bonded threads protected by a lock.
Hydrogen thread: acquire hSem, call releaseHydrogen().
Oxygen thread: acquire oSem, call releaseOxygen().
After releasing, increment the bonded count under a lock; if count == 3, reset count to 0, signal hSem twice and oSem once.
Every thread waits on a per-molecule barrier (e.g., CyclicBarrier / threading.Barrier) before finishing so no thread proceeds into the next molecule early.

c.python:
import threading

class Solution:
    def __init__(self):
        self.h = threading.Semaphore(2)
        self.o = threading.Semaphore(1)
        self.barrier = threading.Barrier(3)

    def hydrogen(self, releaseHydrogen: 'Callable[[], None]') -> None:
        self.h.acquire()
        self.barrier.wait()
        releaseHydrogen()
        self.h.release()

    def oxygen(self, releaseOxygen: 'Callable[[], None]') -> None:
        self.o.acquire()
        self.barrier.wait()
        releaseOxygen()
        self.o.release()

a.t: O(n) total work across all threads — each thread does constant semaphore operations.
a.sp: O(1) extra space — a fixed number of semaphores/counters regardless of n.

a.n: Approach 2: Single Mutex with State Machine
a.i: Guard all shared state with one mutex and condition variables. Keep counters of waiting hydrogens and oxygens that have passed the gate; a molecule forms whenever we have at least one oxygen and two hydrogens queued, at which point we wake exactly those three. This avoids multiple synchronization primitives and makes the invariant explicit in one place.
s: Maintain counts hWaiting, oWaiting and a flag per role under a single mutex.
A hydrogen increments hWaiting and waits on a condition variable until it is selected for a molecule.
An oxygen does the same with oWaiting.
Whenever hWaiting >= 2 and oWaiting >= 1, pick one oxygen and two hydrogens, decrement counts, and notify their condition variables.
Selected threads invoke their release function and return.
a.t: O(n) overall — each thread performs a bounded number of state checks and notifications.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the input — just counters and condition variables.

w: In an interview, lead with Approach 1: it is the canonical answer and maps directly onto Java's Semaphore/CyclicBarrier or Python's threading primitives. The key pitfalls are forgetting the barrier (threads from different molecules interleaving their release calls), initializing the hydrogen semaphore to 2 rather than 1, and deciding which thread resets the counters (any deterministic choice works, but it must happen exactly once per molecule). Edge cases: n = 1 (single molecule), and inputs where all oxygens arrive before any hydrogen — the oxygen must genuinely block, not spin forever. Likely follow-ups: generalize to arbitrary molecule ratios (e.g., H2SO4), avoid busy-waiting in JavaScript (use promises/resolvers instead of polling), and discuss fairness/starvation guarantees.
